intro:
How our stem cell preparation is made

MIRAE STEM CELL — four stages from harvest to application

  1. Harvest — taken from your own bodyA small amount of fat is aspirated. The quantity needed is not large, and it is done under local anaesthesia. The cells used are your own, from beginning to end.
  2. Separation — isolating the stem cells within the fatHarvested fat contains fat cells, vascular cells and stem cells mixed together. Using ultrasound and centrifugation, only the layer responsible for regeneration is separated out. In medical terms this layer is called the stromal vascular fraction (SVF).
  3. Activation — waking the cells with the MCT processThe separated cells undergo an MCT activation process. Inside a cell is a "power station" called the mitochondrion, and the more active it is, the more actively the cell works. MCT is the stage that stimulates this power station so that the cells are ready to work.
    Even with the same stem cells, the state in which they enter the body matters. That is why we keep this as a separate stage.
  4. Application — returned where they are neededYour own activated cells are applied to the target area. Skin, joints, scalp — the method follows the area and purpose agreed at your consultation.
Why do these four stages matter?

Procedures may all be called "stem cell treatment", but where the cells come from (①), how they are separated (②), what state they are put into (③) and where they are placed (④) make them entirely different procedures. When comparing, ask about these four points. We explain all four.

Why people choose us

Only your own material

The material used in our adipose-derived stem cell, PRP and PRF procedures is entirely the patient's own tissue and blood. Since no other person's cells or outside products are introduced, there is no need to worry about rejection of foreign tissue.

A medical team long involved with stem cells

Dr Park Jong-yun has served as director of a cord blood bank and as an advisory professor on cord blood, and is a full member of the Korean Society for Stem Cell Research. A doctor with experience both in storing and managing stem cells and in using them in clinical practice consults with you directly.

Within a single day

As a rule, harvest through to application is completed in one visit. There is no need to travel back and forth to the clinic.

Stem cells are not a difficult idea

The cells of the body fall broadly into two kinds.

One kind is the "working cell". Skin cells make up skin; cartilage cells make up joints. Each has its assigned job.

The other is the "stem cell". It has not yet been decided what it will become. It goes where it is needed and becomes a skin cell, a bone cell or a cartilage cell. It is, in effect, the repair crew that fills in where the body has been damaged.

The difficulty is that with age both the number and the vitality of these repair cells decline. That is why a wound that healed in a few days in your twenties takes weeks in your fifties.

Stem cell treatment is the procedure of gathering those repair cells still remaining somewhere in your body and sending them back to where they are most needed.

Where do stem cells come from?

In an adult body there are broadly three sources.

SourceHow it is obtainedIn a word
FatAspirating a small amount of fatThe largest yield, with the least burden
Bone marrowDrawing marrow from the hip boneThe longest research record, but harvesting is painful
Cord bloodFrom the umbilical cord at birthAvailable only at that moment, so usable only if stored in advance

Of these, we work principally with adipose-derived stem cells, because the burden of harvesting is low while the yield from a single harvest is the greatest.

groups.lead:
Please note first — PRP and PRF are not "stem cells"

This is often confused, so we set it out at the start.

  • Stem cell treatment gathers and introduces the regenerative cells themselves.
  • PRP and PRF are not cells. They gather and introduce the platelets and growth factors in your own blood. They are closer to sending cells a signal to "start working".

Both use material taken from your own body, but what is introduced is different. They are chosen according to purpose, or used together.

tags.d:
What is the procedure?

Drawn blood is spun in a centrifuge and separates into layers. Only the layer in which platelets are concentrated is drawn off and injected into the area that needs it. From blood draw to injection, it is usually completed in one sitting.

Why would it be expected to help?

Platelets contain the growth factors that direct healing when an injury occurs. PRP is understood to concentrate these growth factors to three to five times the level in normal blood. Rather than waiting for the body to send them of its own accord, they are placed directly where healing is needed.

This may suit you if
  • pain in the elbow, shoulder or knee has persisted for a long time
  • you would like to improve the firmness and texture of your skin
  • thinning hair concerns you
Points to be aware of
  • PRP is a preparation made from your own blood, and is distinct from a stem cell preparation.
  • The degree and duration of effect differ by area and by individual condition. The same result does not occur for everyone.
  • For medial and lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow, golfer's elbow), Korean national health insurance coverage applies in some cases. Whether it applies to you is explained at your consultation.

What is the procedure?

It starts in the same way as PRP. The difference is that no anticoagulant is added at all, and the blood is centrifuged immediately after it is drawn. The blood then clots on its own into a jelly-like mesh, and the platelets and growth factors held inside that mesh are what is called PRF.

How does it differ from PRP?
PRPPRF
AnticoagulantAddedNot added
FormLiquid — injectedGel or membrane (injectable forms also exist)
How growth factors are releasedAll at once, on introductionSlowly, from the mesh
As an imagePouring water all at onceLeaving a sponge soaked with water

This slow-release property is exactly why PRF is called a "second-generation platelet concentrate".

This may suit you if
  • you would like the effect of a single procedure to last longer
  • you prefer a method that uses your own blood alone, with no additives
  • a form that can be laid over the area needing regeneration is appropriate
Points to be aware of

Because it is made from your blood alone, the risk of a foreign-body reaction or transmitted infection is relatively low. Results may still differ by individual and by procedure.

Our principal treatment

What is the procedure?

A small amount of fat is aspirated, the stem cells within it are separated, they pass through the MCT activation process, and they are then applied to the same patient. The four stages set out above are this procedure.

Why fat?

Adipose tissue is the place in the body from which stem cells can be obtained in the greatest quantity with the least burden.

  • Harvesting is far simpler than drawing bone marrow.
  • The number of cells obtained at one time is large.
  • They grow well and age relatively slowly compared with cells obtained from bone marrow.
This may suit you if
  • you want general anti-ageing care — skin firmness, lines and so on
  • joint discomfort has been with you for a long time
  • you are considering regenerative effects alongside fat grafting or surgery
Points to be aware of

For cells obtained from fat, the academic criteria for saying definitively "this and only this is a stem cell" are not yet fully established. In practice, therefore, a mixture of cells including stem cells is used. Which approach suits which patient is judged individually at consultation.

What is the procedure?

Marrow is drawn from the hip bone (iliac crest) and concentrated by centrifugation before use. This concentrate is called BMAC.

Characteristics
  • These were the first stem cells to be described, and carry the largest body of research.
  • Harvesting is painful, and the quantity obtained at one time is smaller than from fat.
Recognised status in Korea

Intra-articular injection of bone marrow aspirate concentrate for patients with knee osteoarthritis was listed as a New Health Technology in July 2023 (Ministry of Health and Welfare Notice No. 2023-128). The assessment confirmed pain relief and functional improvement at a level comparable to existing intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection.

What is cord blood?

It is the baby's blood remaining in the vessels of the placenta and umbilical cord after the cord has been cut at birth. It contains two kinds of stem cell.

  • Haematopoietic stem cells — the stem cells that make blood. They are used in transplant treatment for leukaemia, aplastic anaemia and similar conditions.
  • Mesenchymal stem cells — able to differentiate into several tissues, and so used in cell therapy.
Important points
  • Cord blood can be obtained only at the moment of birth. It is therefore available to you and your family only if it was stored at that time.
  • In Korea, cord blood is collected, tested, stored and supplied by licensed cord blood banks under the Act on Management of and Research on Cord Blood. It is not something that may be handled anywhere.

outro:
How the procedure runs

  1. ConsultationSeen by the doctor. We confirm your goals and the area, whether the procedure is suitable, and set out the expected number of sessions and the cost.
  2. HarvestFat or blood is taken, according to purpose. Fat harvesting is done under local anaesthesia.
  3. ProcessingSeparation and activation are carried out. You can rest during this time.
  4. ApplicationThe prepared cells are applied to the target area.
  5. GuidanceWe explain the after-care and the schedule for follow-up.

※ Duration varies with the type of procedure and the area. The exact schedule is given at your consultation.

Frequently asked questions

Are another person's cells introduced?
No. Our adipose stem cell, PRP and PRF procedures use only the patient's own tissue and blood.
Does it hurt a great deal?
Fat harvesting is carried out under local anaesthesia. Drawing blood is at the level of an ordinary blood test. Bone marrow harvesting is comparatively uncomfortable, so we explain it fully in advance at the consultation.
When will I feel the effect?
It varies by area and by individual. Regeneration is a process that takes time, so it more usually appears gradually over weeks rather than immediately after the procedure. Wherever you hear it, an explanation that "you will clearly see a difference within days" is worth judging carefully.
Is one session enough?
It depends on the purpose and your condition. We set out the expected number of sessions and the intervals at the consultation before proceeding.
Are there no side effects?
Every procedure carries risk. Because your own tissue is used, the risk of rejection is relatively low, but bruising, swelling or pain at the harvest site and temporary reactions at the injection site can occur. An explanation that there are "no side effects at all" is hard to trust.
Is it covered by health insurance?
Mostly not. However, PRP for medial and lateral epicondylitis, and intra-articular injection of bone marrow aspirate concentrate for knee osteoarthritis, have recognised scope under the Korean system. Whether it applies in your case is confirmed at the consultation.
Which is better, PRP or stem cells?
Not "better" — different. PRP sends the signal for repair; stem cells introduce the working cells themselves. They are chosen according to purpose, or used together.
Can I have this at an older age?
It is true that both the number and vitality of stem cells decline with age. That is why we assess individual condition before the procedure and then judge suitability.
Does it help with any condition at all?
No. Stem cells are not a cure-all. Different conditions need different approaches. At the consultation we tell you honestly whether this procedure is appropriate, or whether another treatment would be better.
Should I decide quickly?
Not at all. Take the time to look into it thoroughly before deciding. If you wish, you are welcome to seek an opinion from another medical institution as well.

What we tell you before you decide

Regenerative medicine is care you should agree to only after a full explanation. Before any procedure we set out the following. You have the right to ask about these points at any medical institution.

  • whether this procedure is the standard treatment for your condition, and what other options exist
  • where the cells used come from, how they are separated, and by what route they are introduced
  • the specific effect that can be expected, and how that effect will be assessed
  • the risks of the procedure and the possible side effects, and what is done if they occur
  • the evidence behind the procedure, and whether it has national regulatory approval or review
  • the total cost and any costs that may arise in addition
  • how long, and in what way, your progress will be followed afterwards

Please ask about anything you wish. Deciding once you fully understand is the best start to good care.

Further reading — the academic definition of mesenchymal stem cells
The International Society for Cell & Gene Therapy (ISCT) defines the mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC) by the following three minimal criteria.
  1. adherence to plastic under standard culture conditions
  2. positive for CD105, CD73 and CD90, and negative for CD45, CD34, CD14 (or CD11b), CD79a (or CD19) and HLA-DR
  3. the ability to differentiate in vitro into osteoblasts, adipocytes and chondroblasts
